messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] expanding the size of the network
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I have a question about expanding the size of the network.

So for example, if we have data for 200 injection drug users (IDU), and then we want to simulate an IDU network of 2000, and we have dyad-dependent term such as gwesp in the model, wha?t the best way to simulate the expanded network?

I tried to fit the model with the small network, and then initialize a network of 2000 (with node attributes but no edge information) and pass it to the ?network? of the fitted ergm object, and use the updated ergm to simulate, but it didn?t work.

Another way may be to use the egocentric method, that?s first initializing the network of 2000 and then using target stats to estimate/fit ergm, and then simulate from that. If this is the only way, are there built-in functions to calculate the target stats for the network of 2000 from the network of 200? Is there any document on it?

Thank you so much.

Best,
Lin

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Comparing levels of homophily between subsets of edges in the same network
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Comparing levels of homophily between subsets of edges in the same network
messages.body_plain:
Hello Timoth?e --


One idea for something to try here would be to code up one or more new 
ERGM terms for the count of homophilous ties that appear within your 
higher-order configurations of interest.? You could then fit a model 
that had both a basic nodematch term in it and your more specific 
nodematch term in it, and you could see if the latter was positive and 
significant even when the former was in the model. This would give you 
the amount of homophily "boost" associated with the configurations.? The 
trick, of course, is that it requires writing up a new term -- this is 
often not a lot of work, but when your configurations of interest are 
slightly larger -- e.g. cliques of size 4 or above -- them the change 
statistics are less straightforward.? Still doable, though, and starting 
with an existing term /cycle, /and borrowing code from nodematch to put 
into it,//would simplify things dramatically. .? Note that this does 
require a small knowledge of C, although I've been able to mostly fake 
it by combining code from existing terms in most cases. And we have a 
few sets of resources to help, all linked to from 
https://statnet.csde.washington.edu/trac/wiki/Resources. These include a 
dedicated CRAN package (ergm.userterms), and a workshop offered at past 
Sunbelts (see "Archive of previous workshop materials") and tutorial 
(under "statnet User's Guide: JoSS papers on statnet") that both provide 
guidance for that package.

HTH,
Steve


On 11/10/2017 1:13 AM, Chabot, Timoth?e Pierre Jules wrote:
>
> Dear Statnet users,
>
>
> I work on (ethnic) homophily in social networks. An hypothesis I want 
> to test is whether the ties that are embedded in higher level 
> structures are more homophilic, on average, than the ones who are not.
>
>
> From my original network, I can extract only those edges that are 
> reciprocated (ie, symmetrizing the network); then that are part of a 
> full triad ; that are part of a clique of size 4, 5 and so on. In each 
> case, I am interested in comparing the levels of homophily 
> ("nodematch" term) among the edges of the subset with that of the 
> whole network.
>
>
> How can I do this using ERGMs ? Extracting a subset of my network? and 
> estimating an ERGM model with the "nodematch" term for that subset is 
> pretty easy, but how to make sure that the increase in homophily that 
> I may observe in the new subset is not a mechanical result produced by 
> the extraction itself ? For e.g., I guess that if you symmetrize a 
> random network, the homophily rates observed in the symmetrized graph 
> will always be higher than that of the original graph. Is there a way 
> to assess the statistical significance of the increase in homophily 
> that I observe in symmetrical links ?
>
>
> Below is an example using statnet built-in data. I only show it for 
> reciprocal as opposed to all links, but I ask myself the same question 
> about links within triads or cliques.
>
> |library(statnet)library(stargazer)data("faux.dixon.high")net 
> <-faux.dixon.high net.s <-as.sociomatrix(net)net.s 
> <-symmetrize(net.s,rule ="strong")net.s <-network(net.s,directed 
> =F)net.s%v%"race"<-as.character(net%v%"race")m1 <-ergm(net ~edges 
> +nodematch('race'))s1 <-ergm(net.s ~edges 
> +nodematch('race'))stargazer(m1,s1,type="text")# The nodematch 
> coefficient is greater ! Does it mean reciprocal ties are more often 
> homophilic ?summary(net ~edges +nodematch('race'))summary(net.s ~edges 
> +nodematch('race'))912/1197180/219# There is indeed a greater 
> proportion of symmetric ties that are homophilic. But is it significant ?|
>
> At some point I thought that it may be done using interaction effects 
> (modelling the interaction effect between the "mutual" and "nodematch" 
> term in an ERGM model applied to the full network) but I don't know 
> whether the ERGM package can do this. Do you have any ideas or 
> suggestions on how to work around that problem ?
>
>
> Many thanks for the help !
>
>
> Best Regards
>
>
> ---------------------------------
>
> Timoth?e Chabot
>
> PhD Researcher
>
> European University Institute

messages.subject: [statnet_help] expanding the size of the network
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] expanding the size of the network
messages.body_plain:
Hi Lin,

When changing the network size, the key is to update the edges 
coefficient in your model.? The basic idea is to take the edges 
coefficient and add the natural log of the old network size and then 
subtract the natural log of the new network size. Equivalently, one can 
think about partitioning the edges coefficient into two parts: one an 
offset based on the network size and another the remainder, and then 
update the offset. Without this update, ergms will preserve density as 
one changes network size, but with this update, they preserve mean 
degree. Although the former may seem reasonable on first pass, for most 
social phenomena the latter makes muc more sense and matches observed 
behavior much more closely. Note that you do *not* have to update any 
other coefficients besides the edges.

All this is explained in:

Pavel N. Krivitsky, Mark S. Handcock, and Martina Morris (2011). 
Adjusting for Network Size and Composition Effects in Exponential-Family 
Random Graph Models. Statistical Methodology, 8(4): 319?339.

and is also talked about in our Network Modeling for Epidemics course: 
http://statnet.github.io/nme/

Note, however, that Kirivitsky, Handcock and Morris have - in the paper 
below, and in subsequent explorations - proven that this works perfectly 
for dyadic independent terms, and behaves reasonably for some common 
dyadic dependent terms, but haven't proven it works exactly for the 
latter. (Co-authors - correct me if I'm wrong on that!!!)

It's not actually 100% clear (at least to me) what the expected behavior 
should be for something like GWESP when networks change in size - how do 
we believe explicit triangle closure behaves as networks scale in size, 
such that the background probably of a triangle being closed declines 
for the same density? Will the magnitude of the force stay the same, or 
will people exert more effort to close trinagle in order to get back to 
the same prportion of their triangles being closed as in a smaller 
network?? It's tricky stuff, but very intersting, for someone who wanted 
to explore it in depth with comparative empirical data, like Add Health.

Nevertheless, I believe this simple method should get you close to where 
you want to be.

Here is some basic example code using a network of size 100 with mean 
degree of 1, then simulating a network of size 1000 that also has a mean 
degree of 1, by updating the coefficient form the first model. You 
should be able to use this as a base, and add in you GWESP and other terms.

library(statnet)
smallnet <- network.initialize(100, directed=F)
smallnet <- san(smallnet~edges, target.stats = 50) # mean deg = 1
smallergm <- ergm(smallnet~edges)

largenet <- network.initialize(1000, directed=F)
largecoef <- smallergm$coef[1] + log(100) - log(1000)
largenet <- simulate(largenet~edges, coef=largecoef)

Cheers,

Steve

getting my model to converge. I suspect part of the problem is in the

Shane

Hi, Shane,

On Sat, 2017-12-09 at 11:44 -0700, Shane Gleason wrote:
> Hello-

> time 
> getting my model to converge. I suspect part of the problem is in
> the 
> network terms I am using (e.g. nonzero, mutual, etc). The
> documentation 
> directs me to help("ergm-terms").  

Also, it might be worth keeping in mind that valued ERGMs often have
slower mixing, so you might need to increase MCMC sample size and
interval, or use MCMLE.effectiveSize mechanism to try to get them
adaptively.

> However, this file only contains one 
> term.
> 
> Looking through the help file entitled, "Modeling valued networks
> with 
> statnet" (04/16/16) from the Sunbelt 2016 conference ( 
> https://statnet.org/trac/raw-attachment/wiki/Sunbelt2016/Valued.pdf
> ), I 
> am able to come up with a few other terms.  However, I am curious if 
> there is a full list of all the  ergm-terms avaiable for the
> ergm.count 
> somewhere?
> 

Most of the valued terms are usable for data other than counts (though
what they mean might be a work in progress), so they are actually in
the ergm package. help('ergm-terms', package="ergm") will get you the
list of terms implemented, and some of them will be tagged "(valued)".

					I hope this helps,
					Pavel

messages.body_plain:
GreifOlution: Greifswald Summer School for PhD-students, PostDocs and advanced graduate students from 16/09/2018 to 22/09/2018 in Greifswald, Germany

As part of the "Year of Mathematical Biology" we proudly announce GreifOlution, the 1st Greifswald Summer School on Mathematics of Evolution (kindly funded by the DAAD, the German Academic Exchange Service).
The main focus of this summer school will be on mathematical models and methods for reconstructing phylogenetic trees and networks, but upon request we might also include some sessions on other related topics, e.g. from population genetics.
 
So if you are a mathematician or computer scientist with a strong interest in biology or a biologist who aspires to a deeper understanding of mathematical or statistical methods and  models, this summer school is what you need! 
 
Greifswald University is one of the hotspots of mathematical phylogenetics and biomathematics in Germany - as the only German university which has been offering a biomathematics study program already for 20 years, the small town located directly at the Baltic Sea has attracted lots of renowned researchers over the years!
So why not benefit from the presence of all these experts? Come and spend a week in summer at the beautiful Baltic Sea and deepen your knowledge on mathematical phylogenetics!

This summer school aims at bridging the gap between mathematics and biology and providing both a broad introduction to various fields of biomathematics (e.g. biostatistics, bioinformatics and mathematical phylogenetics) as well as insights into state-of-the-art research. 
 
We invite applications from PhD students, PostDocs and advanced graduate students of Mathematics, Computer Science or Biology (and related areas of study) who have a great interest in Biomathematics, in particular in Mathematical Phylogenetics.
The school is free of charge. There are also no costs for the social dinner, the excursions and lunch during the summer school, but participants must cover their own accomodation and travel expenses. Foreign participants, however, may be eligible for funding (see the below for the DAAD reglementation concerning foreign participants).

For more details, please visit https://math-inf.uni-greifswald.de/institut/ueber-uns/mitarbeitende/fischer/greifolution/ 

or contact us at greifolution@uni-greifswald.de


We would be pleased to welcome you in Greifswald in September 2018!

Kind regards,
Mareike Fischer
